item.description: Jim Henson’s The Muppets have always been at their best when they’re treating showbiz like a playground and not a blockbuster obligation. Disney learned that the hard way after buying the brand in 2004 for $75 million and then spending the next two decades toggling between theatrical swings and TV-safe chaos. The big-screen returns — “The Muppets” and “Muppets Most Wanted” — were charming, but they never really became the kind of mega-franchise tentpoles Disney tends to demand. Continue reading

item.title: Josh Safdie Calls ‘Marty Supreme’ A “Heist Film On Fate” In 40 Min Talk With Ben Affleck
item.description: For all the sweaty propulsion and picaresque chaos people tend to ascribe to filmmaker Josh Safdie (“Uncut Gems”), the thing that usually drives his stories is pretty straightforward: desire, frustration, and the better-or-worse refusal to accept “no” for an answer. That was the wavelength he was on when he discussed “Marty Supreme” on the DGA’s The Director’s Cut podcast, where he framed the film’s core not as sports-movie uplift, but as something closer to existential burglary.
